scenes.title: 1. hook (the well that shouldn't go cloudy)
scenes.narration: Here's a result that nearly fooled a student. She's testing unknown C for chloride. She acidifies a few drops with nitric acid, adds silver nitrate, and a faint white cloud appears. Chloride? But in the next well, she'd put plain water and the same reagents, and that well went cloudy too. If the water does it, the cloud can't prove anything about the unknown. She'd rinsed the plate with tap water, and tap water carries a little chloride. That one extra well saved her conclusion.

scenes.title: 2. the aim and the plan
scenes.narration: The aim: identify the cation and the anion in each of four unknown solutions, where each holds one of each from the syllabus lists. Plan before you pick up a dropper: list the tests in order, from the two flowcharts, and what each result would mean. In every row of wells, only the solution changes. That's your independent variable, and what you see is the dependent variable. Everything else stays the same.

scenes.title: 3. blank, known, unknown
scenes.narration: Now the controls. A blank, or negative control, is distilled water with the reagent. It should show no change. If it does, the reagent or the equipment is adding something, like that tap water. A known, or positive control, is a solution you know holds the ion, with the same reagent. It shows the test works today, and what a positive looks like on your plate. So each reagent gets one row: blank, known, unknown. And rinse everything with distilled water, never tap water.

scenes.title: 4. small scale, set up safely
scenes.narration: Run it small. A well plate, like the one from the solubility practical in Module 5, takes three drops of solution and three of reagent. That means less silver, lead and barium to handle, and less waste. Keep the dropper tip above the well, so it never carries one solution back into a bottle. Put a black card under the wells to see white solids, and a white tile to judge colours.

scenes.title: 5. unknown C: the cation
scenes.narration: Unknown C, cation first, with fresh drops in each well. Dilute hydrochloric acid: no visible change, which rules out silver, and usually lead. Dilute sulfuric acid: no change, so not barium. Sodium hydroxide: a white precipitate that stays when you add more. That points to magnesium, or to calcium from a concentrated sample. So, a flame test. Clean the loop in acid and heat it until the flame shows no colour. That's your blank flame. Then the sample: still no colour, so not calcium, which gives brick red. It's magnesium, and the known magnesium well looks just the same.

scenes.title: 6. unknown C: the anion
scenes.narration: Then the anion, again with fresh drops. Dilute nitric acid: no fizz, so no carbonate. Nitric acid, then barium chloride: a white precipitate that stays in the acid, so sulfate. Nitric acid, then silver nitrate: with the plate rinsed in distilled water, the blank stays clear, and so does unknown C. No chloride after all. Each bottle holds one anion, so unknown C is magnesium sulfate.

scenes.title: 7. record as you go
scenes.narration: Record as you go, in a table you drew up before you started. One row per well: the solution, the reagent, what you saw, and only then, in its own column, what it means. Write each observation in full. No visible change, written in, never left blank. Note anything that changes with time, like a green solid that browns in air. An observation is evidence. An inference is your reading of it, so keep them apart.

scenes.title: 8. justify the identity
scenes.narration: When you report an identity, give the evidence and the chemistry. For magnesium: sodium hydroxide gave a white precipitate that stayed in excess, magnesium ions and hydroxide ions form solid magnesium hydroxide, the colourless flame rules out calcium, and the known matched. One more honest limit: no visible change means not detected. A very dilute ion can slip past, so say what your tests can and can't rule out.

scenes.title: 9. valid, reliable, accurate?
scenes.narration: Now the three words from the practical skills video. Valid? Each test should detect only the ion it's meant to. Nitric acid before silver, fresh drops, distilled water and a clear blank all protect that. Reliable? Repeat each deciding test with fresh drops, and compare with another group. Accurate? Here, the result is an identity, so accurate means it's the true one. Matching the known side by side gets you close, and the teacher's key at the end checks it.

scenes.title: 10. the risk assessment
scenes.narration: Now the risks. Silver nitrate stains skin brown-black for days and can damage eyes, so wear gloves and glasses. Lead salts are toxic and may harm an unborn child, and barium salts are toxic if swallowed, so your teacher prepares the dilute solutions and you use them by the drop. Sodium hydroxide and dilute nitric acid can burn eyes and skin. Leave concentrated ammonia to the fume cupboard, and let the hot loop cool on a heatproof mat. Silver residues go into the silver waste, lead and barium into heavy-metal waste, never the sink.

scenes.title: 11. memory aid
scenes.narration: One line for every reagent: blank, known, unknown. The blank shows the reagent adds nothing. The known shows what a positive looks like. Then the unknown is judged against both.

scenes.title: 12. attempt 1 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.narration: Your turn. A student flame-tests four unknowns with one wire loop, rinsing it in water between samples. All four flames are blue-green, and she concludes all four contain copper. Evaluate her conclusion, and propose an improvement. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 13. feedback 1 (brief)
scenes.narration: Not valid. A water rinse may not clean copper off the loop, so copper from the first sample could colour every later flame. Before each sample, clean the loop in dilute hydrochloric acid and heat it until the flame shows no colour. Then confirm with a precipitate: pale blue with sodium hydroxide. Just repeating the flame tests is the trap: the same dirty loop gives the same result.

scenes.title: 14. attempt 2 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.narration: Last one. Unknown E's results are on the card, with the blanks and knowns. Identify both ions, justify each identity, and write one net ionic equation. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 15. feedback 2 (brief)
scenes.narration: Calcium chloride. The white sulfate means barium or calcium, and the brick-red flame, matching the known, decides it: calcium. For the anion, a white silver precipitate in nitric acid that dissolves in dilute ammonia, with a clear blank, supports chloride: silver ions and chloride ions form solid silver chloride. Writing only "tested with silver nitrate" is the slip. Say what you saw.

scenes.title: 16. decision rule and handoff
scenes.narration: So, for any unknown: plan the tests from the flowcharts, run blank, known and unknown side by side at small scale, record what you see before what it means, and justify each identity with an observation and an equation. Next: you know which ion is there. But how much? Colour and light can tell you.

scenes.title: 17. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
scenes.narration: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.title: 1. hook (one you can see, one you can't)
scenes.narration: Two beakers of tap water look exactly the same. One holds lead above the drinking water guideline, just a few millionths of a gram in every litre. You can't see that, and no precipitate test would show so little. Now a copper solution: the deeper the blue, the more copper. Both are questions about how much, and light can answer both. So how do colour and absorption measure concentration?

scenes.title: 2. which light?
scenes.narration: You met the colourimeter in Module 5. Light passes through a cuvette, the solution absorbs some of it, and the meter reports absorbance. A blank sets zero, and absorbance rises in step with concentration. So which light should you use? A copper solution looks blue because it absorbs orange and red light and lets the blue through. So you measure with the colour it absorbs, not the colour you see. In a colourimeter, that's a red or orange filter.

scenes.title: 3. UV-visible: one wavelength, and a spectrum
scenes.narration: A filter lets through a whole band of colours, though. A UV-visible spectrophotometer does better. Inside, a grating spreads the light into a rainbow, and a narrow slit picks out one wavelength. It reaches into ultraviolet too, so some colourless substances can be measured. Step through the wavelengths, measuring at each, and you get an absorption spectrum. For the deep blue copper ammonia complex, the peak sits near six hundred nanometres, in the orange. Measure there, at the peak, called lambda max. Absorbance changes most with concentration at the peak, and the top is fairly flat, so a tiny slip in wavelength barely changes the reading.

scenes.title: 4. a complex makes the colour stronger
scenes.narration: Why use the ammonia complex at all? Copper ions in water are pale blue and absorb only weakly. Ammonia molecules bond around each copper ion, making the deep blue complex from the cation video, and it absorbs several times more strongly. So even low concentrations give a clear reading. Add the ammonia in excess, to the standards and the sample alike, so every copper ion ends up in the complex.

scenes.title: 5. Beer-Lambert as a calculation
scenes.narration: The law behind this is Beer-Lambert: A equals epsilon l c. Say a solution reads an absorbance of point four eight zero, epsilon is a hundred and twenty litres per mole per centimetre, and the cuvette is one centimetre wide. Rearrange for c, absorbance over epsilon times l, and that's point zero zero four zero zero moles per litre. A book value of epsilon may not suit your instrument's light, though, so chemists usually trust a calibration line made on their own instrument.

scenes.title: 6. AAS: atomise, then absorb
scenes.narration: Lead ions are colourless, and far too dilute for any colour test. So for metals at trace levels, chemists use atomic absorption spectroscopy, or AAS. The sample is sprayed into a flame. The water evaporates, and the heat breaks the lead compounds apart into free lead atoms. That's called atomising. A hollow cathode lamp, with its cathode made of lead, shines lead's own wavelengths through the flame. Lead atoms absorb those wavelengths as their electrons jump to higher energy levels, and the detector measures how much light went missing.

scenes.title: 7. why AAS is specific
scenes.narration: Other atoms in the flame need different energies, so they let lead's light pass. You've seen these energy jumps before. In a flame test, heated atoms give out their own colours. In AAS, atoms in the flame take in those same wavelengths from the lamp. So AAS measures atoms in the flame, not ions in the solution. That makes it specific, and sensitive enough for trace metals. The costs: one lamp means one element at a time, and other substances in the sample can change how many atoms form, so standards should resemble the sample.

scenes.title: 8. calibration: standards first
scenes.narration: Like the colourimeter, AAS gives absorbance, not concentration, so it needs a calibration. Standards first, unknown second. Run a blank, then lead standards from point five to two milligrams per litre, and plot absorbance against concentration. The points fall close to a straight line. Now an unknown can be read across, then down, as long as its reading sits inside the standards.

scenes.title: 9. worked example: out of range, so dilute
scenes.narration: Here's a factory discharge tested for lead. Its first reading is above the top standard. Don't stretch the line past the last point, because nothing shows it stays straight out there. Dilute it instead: twenty five millilitres made up to two hundred and fifty, a tenfold dilution. Now it reads point one one three, inside the range.

scenes.title: 10. worked example: read, then multiply back
scenes.narration: Now read it. The line's gradient is point one six two absorbance units per milligram per litre, so divide: point one one three over point one six two gives point six nine eight milligrams per litre. But that's the diluted solution. Multiply back by the dilution factor, ten, and the discharge holds six point nine eight milligrams of lead per litre.

scenes.title: 11. which method?
scenes.narration: So which method? If the species is coloured, or can be made coloured with a complex, colourimetry is quick and cheap, and UV-visible is more selective, with one chosen wavelength. For one metal at trace levels, coloured or not, choose AAS.

scenes.title: 12. memory aid
scenes.narration: Two lines to keep. Read across, then down, only inside the standards, then multiply back by the dilution factor. And in AAS, the lamp is made of the element you're testing.

scenes.title: 13. attempt 1 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.narration: Your turn. Copper in vineyard runoff is measured by AAS. Ten millilitres was diluted to one hundred, and the diluted solution reads point two two six. Use the calibration to find the copper concentration in the original runoff. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 14. feedback 1 (brief)
scenes.narration: Read point two two six across to the line and down: about two point five milligrams per litre. That's the diluted solution. The runoff was diluted tenfold, so multiply by ten: about twenty five milligrams per litre. Stopping at two point five is the classic slip, because that's the diluted value.

scenes.title: 15. attempt 2 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.narration: Last one. Two samples: a deep blue copper ammonia solution, and tap water to be checked for traces of lead. Choose a technique for each, and justify your choice. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 16. feedback 2 (brief)
scenes.narration: For the copper complex, colourimetry or UV-visible: it's strongly coloured, so it absorbs visible light, best measured at lambda max. For trace lead, AAS: lead is colourless, and only lead atoms absorb the lead lamp's light, so it's specific and sensitive. Saying AAS detects the lead ions in the water is the trap. It measures atoms in the flame.

scenes.title: 17. handoff
scenes.narration: So, to measure concentration with light, pick a method your species responds to, calibrate with standards, read inside the range, and correct for any dilution. Next, you'll build a calibration yourself, from standards to an unknown.

scenes.title: 18. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
scenes.narration: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.title: 1. hook (colour into a number)
scenes.narration: Two blue solutions. Your eye can tell which one is darker, but not how much copper is in either. A calibration turns that colour into a number. You measure how much light some solutions of known concentration absorb, draw the line they make, then read a sample you don't know straight off that line. Today you build one for copper, and use it on rinse water from a copper plating workshop.

scenes.title: 2. the aim and the variables
scenes.narration: The aim is to find the concentration of copper ions in that rinse water. Each solution whose concentration you know is called a standard. The independent variable is the standards' concentration. The dependent variable is their absorbance, how much light each one soaks up. Everything else stays the same.

scenes.title: 3. make the standards
scenes.narration: Start from a stock solution of copper sulfate, point two zero zero moles per litre. Fill one burette with stock and another with distilled water, rinsing each with the liquid it will hold. Run one millilitre of stock and nine of water into a tube, and mix. That's a tenfold dilution, so point zero two zero moles per litre. Two, three and four millilitres of stock give the next three standards, and six millilitres gives a stronger fifth, point one two zero.

scenes.title: 4. which light, and the blank
scenes.narration: Which light? A blue solution absorbs at the red end of the spectrum. A scan of one standard shows its biggest absorbance near eight hundred nanometres, so set the instrument there. That's where each small change in copper gives the biggest change in absorbance. Then zero it with a blank, a cuvette of the same distilled water. The glass and the water absorb a little too, and the blank takes that away, so what's left comes from copper.

scenes.title: 5. measure carefully
scenes.narration: Hold each cuvette by its ridged sides, and wipe the clear sides, because a fingerprint scatters light and adds absorbance. Rinse the cuvette with the next standard before you fill it, so the last one doesn't dilute it. Keep it facing the same way every time, and work from the most dilute to the most concentrated.

scenes.title: 6. plot it, and find the linear range
scenes.narration: Here are the readings. Plot absorbance up the side and concentration along the bottom, with the blank as a point at zero. The blank and the first four standards sit close to one straight line. The fifth falls well below it. At high absorbance, so little light reaches the detector that the reading is less trustworthy. So this line only holds up to point zero eight zero moles per litre. That's its linear range.

scenes.title: 7. the unknown is too strong
scenes.narration: Now the rinse water. It reads one point five two, far above the top of the linear range. You could extend the line, but the fifth standard has just shown that the line bends up there, so don't trust it. Dilute it instead. Five millilitres of rinse water and five of distilled water halve its concentration. Three readings now give a mean of point eight four five, inside the range.

scenes.title: 8. read it, then scale back
scenes.narration: Read across from point eight four five to the line, then down: point zero seven one zero moles per litre. That's the diluted solution, though. You halved it, so the rinse water is double that, point one four two moles per litre.

scenes.title: 9. reliable, and accurate?
scenes.narration: Reliable? The three readings agree within about point zero zero six, and a second dilution gives the same answer. Accurate? Your teacher made a check standard from a separate weighing, point zero five zero zero moles per litre. Read from your line, it comes out at point zero four nine seven, within about one percent of its true value. It's the same idea as testing a gravimetric method on a sample you already know.

scenes.title: 10. is it valid?
scenes.narration: Valid? The method measures copper only if copper is the only thing absorbing at that wavelength. A cloudy sample scatters light and reads high, so filter it first. And the unknown has to be read at the same wavelength, in the same cuvette, zeroed with the same blank, and inside the linear range. Then the standards' line applies to it.

scenes.title: 11. the risk assessment
scenes.narration: Now the risks. Copper sulfate is harmful if swallowed, irritates eyes and skin, and is very toxic to aquatic life. Wear gloves and glasses, and every copper solution goes into heavy-metal waste, never the sink. Treat the rinse water the same way, because it may hold acid or other metals. Fill the burettes below eye level, and fill cuvettes away from the instrument, so a spill can't reach its electronics.

scenes.title: 12. memory aid
scenes.narration: Two lines to keep. Read across, then down, and only inside the standards. And if you diluted it, multiply back by the dilution factor.

scenes.title: 13. attempt 1 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.narration: Your turn. A student's copper standards give the calibration line on screen. Ten millilitres of an unknown copper solution is diluted to twenty five millilitres, and the diluted solution reads point three two five. Calculate the copper ion concentration in the original solution. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 14. feedback 1 (brief)
scenes.narration: Read across from point three two five, then down: point two five zero moles per litre. That's the diluted solution. Twenty five over ten is a dilution factor of two point five, so the original is point six two five moles per litre. The trap is stopping at point two five zero.

scenes.title: 15. attempt 2 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.narration: Last one. A student measures the standards in a clean cuvette, then measures the unknown in a cuvette with a fingerprint on one clear side. Explain how this affects the calculated concentration, and propose an improvement. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 16. feedback 2 (brief)
scenes.narration: The fingerprint scatters some light, so less reaches the detector, and the absorbance reads high. A higher absorbance, read from the line, gives a concentration that's too high. Fix it by holding cuvettes by their ridged sides and wiping the clear sides before every reading. The trap is averaging three readings. Each one still has the fingerprint, so they're all high together.

scenes.title: 17. decision rule and handoff
scenes.narration: So, to trust a calibration: make your standards by careful dilution, zero with a blank, set the wavelength the solution absorbs most, and keep the unknown inside the linear range, diluting it if you must. Then check accuracy with a standard you already know. Next: calibration and water-analysis data practice.

scenes.title: 18. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
scenes.narration: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.title: 1. hook
scenes.narration: A calibration graph turns an absorbance into a concentration, but exam questions add a twist. The sample reads above the standards. The line doesn't start at zero. Or the result is right, but it's from the wrong sample for the question being asked. Here are three HSC-style questions on water samples. Pause and try each one, then we'll work through it together.

scenes.title: 2a. q1-question (question 1: AAS calibration with a dilution)
scenes.narration: Question one. Copper standards are measured by atomic absorption spectroscopy, and the readings are on screen. A sample of mine drainage water gives an absorbance of point six two zero. The student then dilutes ten millilitres of it to fifty millilitres, and the diluted solution reads point one four two. Construct the calibration graph, explain why the sample was diluted, and calculate the copper concentration in the drainage water. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 2b. q1-graph (draw it)
scenes.narration: Part a. The standards' concentration was chosen, so it goes along the bottom, with absorbance up the side. Use even steps that fill the grid, label both axes with units, and plot each point as a small cross. Then rule one straight line of best fit through the points, including the blank, not dot to dot. These points sit almost exactly on it, and the slope is about point one absorbance for each milligram per litre.

scenes.title: 2c. q1-range (why dilute)
scenes.narration: Part b. The top standard reads about point four. The undiluted sample, at point six two zero, is well above it, outside the standards. Nothing in this data shows the line stays straight up there, and atomic absorption calibrations often bend at high concentration. So the student diluted it, to bring the reading back inside the range the standards cover.

scenes.title: 2d. q1-calc (read it, then multiply back)
scenes.narration: Part c. Read across from point one four two to the line, then down, and show those read-off lines: one point four two milligrams per litre. That's the diluted solution. Fifty over ten is a dilution factor of five, so the drainage water holds about seven point one milligrams per litre.

scenes.title: 2e. q1-mistake (the classic mistake)
scenes.narration: The classic slip is extending the line up to point six two zero. That gives about six point two, nearly one milligram per litre below the diluted result, because the real response bends below the straight line up there. Outside the standards, doubt the line. Dilute and remeasure.

scenes.title: 3a. q2-question (question 2: a line with an intercept)
scenes.narration: Question two. Iron in bore water is measured by colourimetry. A reagent turns the iron into an orange-red complex, and the same amount of reagent goes into every standard and into the sample. The instrument was zeroed with distilled water. The calibration line and its equation are on screen, and the bore water reads point two nine zero. Explain why the zero standard has an absorbance, then calculate the iron concentration in the bore water. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 3b. q2-blank (why the line starts above zero)
scenes.narration: Part a. The zero standard has no added iron, but it still reads point zero three two. It does contain the reagent, and the instrument was zeroed with plain water, not with the reagent. So something in the reagent absorbs a little, perhaps a trace of iron in the chemicals themselves. Every standard and the sample carry that same extra point zero three two. That's why the line starts above zero.

scenes.title: 3c. q2-calc (subtract, then divide)
scenes.narration: Part b. Take the reagent's share off first. Point two nine zero minus point zero three two is point two five eight. That's the absorbance from the bore water's iron. Divide by the slope, point one nine nine, and you get about one point three zero milligrams per litre. Reading across to the line and down gives the same answer.

scenes.title: 3d. q2-mistake (the classic mistake)
scenes.narration: The classic slip is dividing point two nine zero by the slope straight away. That gives about one point four six, too high, because it counts the reagent's absorbance as iron. When a line has an intercept, subtract it before you divide. Better still, zero the instrument with a reagent blank, a cuvette holding every reagent but no iron.

scenes.title: 4a. q3-question (question 3: judge the monitoring evidence)
scenes.narration: Question three. A school tests the lead in water from one drinking bubbler. A sample taken first thing in the morning, after the water stood in the pipes overnight, contains point zero one two milligrams per litre. A sample taken after the bubbler ran for two minutes contains point zero zero two. The school claims the water is safe to drink, because the flushed sample is under the guideline value. Evaluate this claim. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 4b. q3-data (compare each result)
scenes.narration: Start with the method. Can it measure lead at this level? Its detection limit, the lowest concentration it can reliably measure, is point zero zero one, five times below the guideline, so yes. Now the morning sample. Point zero one two over point zero zero five is about two point four times the guideline. The flushed sample is under it. So lead is probably dissolving into the water while it stands in the pipes and fittings.

scenes.title: 4c. q3-claim (evaluate the claim)
scenes.narration: Now the claim. The flushed result is real, but it isn't the water many students drink. The first drink of the day comes after the water has stood overnight, and that sample was over the guideline. And one bubbler on one day doesn't show what the others do. So the claim isn't supported. The school could flush the bubblers each morning, retest every bubbler over several days, and replace the fittings the lead comes from.

scenes.title: 4d. q3-mistake (the classic mistake)
scenes.narration: The trap is averaging the two results. Point zero zero seven sounds like a fair middle, but the two samples answer different questions: one is the water after it stands, the other after it runs. Their average describes no water anyone actually drinks. Match the sample to the question.

scenes.title: 5. decision-board
scenes.narration: So, for any calibration or monitoring question. Read the unknown only inside the standards, and dilute it if it's above them. Multiply back by every dilution. If the line has an intercept, subtract it before you divide. And judge a result with the sample that matches the question, which water, when and where, and not from one sample alone. Next: why monitor water and nutrient pollution?

scenes.title: 6. key-notes (reuse take: key-notes; quiet, about 60 seconds)
scenes.narration: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.title: 1. hook (an invisible loss, a visible bubble)
scenes.narration: You can't see water vapour leaving a leaf. But you can watch a tiny air bubble creep along a glass tube as a leafy shoot draws water in. In still air, it moves about four millimetres a minute. With a fan on, it moves more than twice as fast. So how do you test this fairly, and what does the bubble really tell you?

scenes.title: 2. why uptake tracks loss
scenes.narration: Recall how plants lose water. Water evaporates inside the leaves and diffuses out through the stomata, and more water is pulled up the xylem to replace it. So the faster a leafy shoot loses water, the faster its stem draws water in. Measuring what goes in lets you estimate what comes out.

scenes.title: 3. the potometer
scenes.narration: That's the job of a potometer, a device that measures how fast a shoot takes up water. The cut shoot is sealed into a tube of water, joined to a narrow glass tube with a scale. As the shoot draws water in, the water column moves towards it, carrying a small air bubble along. The distance the bubble moves in a set time gives the rate of uptake. A reservoir lets you push the bubble back to the start.

scenes.title: 4. airtight, settled
scenes.narration: Any leak means the bubble no longer tracks what the shoot takes in, so the set-up must be airtight. Cut the shoot under water, so air can't enter the xylem and block it, and fit it in under water too. Seal the joints with petroleum jelly, blot the leaves dry, and let the shoot settle for about five minutes before timing.

scenes.title: 5. aim and variables
scenes.narration: The aim: find out how air movement affects the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot. The independent variable is air movement, fan off or fan on. The dependent variable is the rate, how far the bubble moves per minute. Keep everything else the same: the same shoot, so the leaf area can't change, the same room, temperature and light, and the same fan distance.

scenes.title: 6. the control and repeats
scenes.narration: Still air is the control, the comparison without the fan. Time the bubble over five minutes, push it back, and repeat three times for each condition. After switching the fan on, let the shoot settle at its new rate before timing again.

scenes.title: 7. taking a reading
scenes.narration: Here's one reading. In still air, the bubble moved twenty one millimetres in five minutes. Rate is distance divided by time, so that's four point two millimetres per minute. Read the same edge of the bubble each time, with your eye level with the tube.

scenes.title: 8. the results
scenes.narration: Here are all six. In still air, four point two, three point eight and four point oh, a mean of four. With the fan, nine point four, nine point two and nine point six, a mean of nine point four. The repeats agree within about half a millimetre per minute, and the gap is more than five. So with the fan, this shoot took up water a little more than twice as fast. Moving air sweeps the moist air from the leaf surface, so vapour diffuses out faster.

scenes.title: 9. what the bubble really measures
scenes.narration: Be careful what you claim. A potometer measures water uptake, not water loss. Most of the water taken in is lost by transpiration, but a little is used in photosynthesis or stays in the cells. And this is one cut shoot with no roots, not a whole plant in a windy paddock. So keep the conclusion narrow: with moving air, this shoot took up water faster than in still air.

scenes.title: 10. a second method: counting stomata
scenes.narration: A second method asks a different question: where can water leave? Paint clear nail varnish on a leaf, let it dry, and lift it off with clear tape. This peel keeps an imprint of the surface. Under a microscope, count the stomata in one field of view, lower surface, then upper. Here, about twenty against three. But a count can't show whether the pores are open, so it shows where water can leave, not how fast.

scenes.title: 11. validity, reliability and accuracy
scenes.narration: Now judge it with three questions. Validity: does it measure what it was meant to? Only the air movement changed, on one settled shoot, so it fairly tests uptake, which is close to water loss but not the same. Reliability: if you repeat it, do the results agree? Yes, within about half a millimetre per minute. Accuracy: how close to the true value? A slow leak shifts every reading, and more repeats can't fix a leak.

scenes.title: 12. risk assessment
scenes.narration: The risk assessment. Cut stems on a tile, away from your fingers, because a sharp blade can slip. Keep the fan and its cord away from the water, and mop up spills, to avoid an electric shock. Nail varnish is flammable and its fumes irritate, so use a little, in a ventilated room, away from flames.

scenes.title: 13a. attempt 1 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.narration: Your turn. A student used a potometer on one leafy shoot, with and without a clear plastic bag over its leaves. Without the bag, the bubble moved thirty millimetres in six minutes. With the bag, it moved twelve millimetres in six minutes. Calculate both rates, then explain the difference. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 13b. feedback 1 (brief)
scenes.narration: Thirty divided by six is five millimetres per minute without the bag, and twelve divided by six is two with it. Inside the bag, water vapour builds up, so the air around the leaves gets very humid. The vapour difference between leaf and air is smaller, so vapour diffuses out more slowly, and the shoot takes up less. The classic mistake is saying the bag blocks the water. It traps humid air.

scenes.title: 13c. attempt 2 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.narration: One more. A student cut a shoot in the air and pushed it into a potometer. She measured the rate with a fan on a warm Monday afternoon, and in still air on a cool Tuesday morning, then concluded that wind increases transpiration. Identify two problems, and propose a change that fixes each one. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 13d. feedback 2 (brief)
scenes.narration: One: cutting in air lets air into the xylem, which can block uptake, so cut and fit the shoot under water. Two: the temperature changed as well as the fan, so the difference could come from the temperature. Test both with the same shoot, in the same room, on the same day. The classic mistake is to repeat it more times. Repeats help reliability, but they can't fix an uncontrolled variable.

scenes.title: 14. decision rule and handoff
scenes.narration: So for any transpiration practical: change one factor, keep the shoot and everything else the same, seal it airtight, let it settle, repeat each reading, and claim only what you measured, the uptake by this shoot. Next: practical questions, and fixes that fix.

scenes.title: 15. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
scenes.narration: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.title: 1. hook (what Australians die of)
scenes.narration: Around 1900, many Australians died of diseases they caught from someone else, like pneumonia and tuberculosis. Today, most Australians die of diseases nobody can catch: heart disease, dementia, stroke and lung cancer. That's partly because vaccines, antibiotics and clean water now prevent many deaths from infection, so more people live long enough for these slower diseases to develop. So if a disease isn't caught, what causes it?

scenes.title: 2. the dividing line
scenes.narration: Start with the dividing line. An infectious disease is caused by a pathogen, like a bacterium or virus, that can pass from one host to another. A non-infectious disease has no pathogen passing it on, so you can't catch it. That's the test. It isn't about how serious the disease is, or whether genes are involved. Cystic fibrosis is genetic, and it's still non-infectious, because no pathogen passes it between people.

scenes.title: 3. four groups of cause
scenes.narration: So what does cause them? The causes fall into four groups. A genetic disease starts with a change in DNA that alters a protein. An environmental disease starts with something from outside the body that damages cells. A nutritional disease comes from too little, or too much, of a nutrient. And cancer is cells dividing out of control. For each one, trace the same chain: the cause, what changes in the cells, and the effect on the body.

scenes.title: 4. cystic fibrosis: the normal job
scenes.narration: Start with a genetic disease, cystic fibrosis. Cells lining your airways make a protein called CFTR, from the CFTR gene. It's a channel in the cell membrane that lets chloride ions out onto the airway surface. Water follows the chloride by osmosis, so the mucus there stays thin and runny, and tiny hairs called cilia sweep it, with any trapped bacteria, up and out.

scenes.title: 5. what goes wrong
scenes.narration: In cystic fibrosis, both copies of the CFTR gene are altered. The most common change removes one amino acid, so the protein folds the wrong way, and the cell breaks it down before it reaches the membrane. With too few channels, less chloride leaves the cells, so less water follows. The mucus dries out and turns thick and sticky. The cilia can't clear it, bacteria stay trapped, and the lungs get repeated infections.

scenes.title: 6. effect, not cause; inherited, not caught
scenes.narration: Notice the order. Thick mucus is the effect near the end of the chain, not the cause. The cause is the altered gene, then the faulty protein. And because cystic fibrosis needs two altered copies, two healthy carriers can have a child with it. It runs in families, but it's inherited, not caught.

scenes.title: 7. environmental: silicosis
scenes.narration: An environmental disease starts outside the body. Cutting engineered stone, used for kitchen benchtops, releases fine silica dust, which can be breathed deep into the lungs. Immune cells there take up the particles but can't break them down, and the damage leads to scar tissue. Scarred lungs are stiff, so breathing gets harder. That's silicosis. The dust caused it, and nobody caught it from anyone. The next video looks at exposures like this in detail.

scenes.title: 8. nutritional: iron-deficiency anaemia
scenes.narration: A nutritional disease comes from the diet. Iron is part of haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. With too little iron, the body makes less haemoglobin, so red blood cells come out smaller and paler, and the blood carries less oxygen. That's iron-deficiency anaemia, which can leave someone tired and short of breath. Too much of a nutrient can cause disease as well, and that's coming up soon.

scenes.title: 9. cancer: melanoma
scenes.narration: Cancer gets its own group, because it's defined by what the cells do, not by what started it. Genes normally control when a cell divides. When enough of those control genes are damaged, a cell keeps dividing, forms a lump called a tumour, and can invade nearby tissue. The damage can start in different ways. Melanoma, a skin cancer, is mainly triggered by ultraviolet light, so it's a cancer with an environmental trigger. Name the group first, then the trigger.

scenes.title: 10. several causes at once
scenes.narration: Real diseases often have several causes acting together. Type 2 diabetes involves inherited genes, diet, activity and age, all pushing the same way. That's called multifactorial. So when you classify a disease, name its main contributing factor, then explain how that factor changes cells.

scenes.title: 11a. attempt one (classify and resolve)
scenes.narration: Two exam questions. First. Three conditions are described on screen: goitre, Huntington's disease and cervical cancer. Classify each one into a group. Then explain why a student who says cervical cancer is infectious is wrong. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 11b. feedback, item one
scenes.narration: Goitre is nutritional: too little iodine, so the thyroid can't make enough hormone and enlarges. Huntington's is genetic: an altered gene leads to a harmful protein. Cervical cancer is a cancer, with an infectious trigger. The virus can pass between people, but the cancer itself can't. The classic mistake is thinking a virus is involved, so it's infectious. Ask what passes between people.

scenes.title: 11c. attempt two (trace a genetic disease)
scenes.narration: Second. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is caused by an altered LDLR gene. Normally, this gene codes for a receptor on liver cells that removes LDL cholesterol from the blood. Explain how the altered gene can lead to heart disease. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 11d. feedback, item two
scenes.narration: The altered gene means fewer working LDL receptors on liver cells. So the liver removes less LDL, and LDL cholesterol builds up in the blood. Over years it's deposited in artery walls, narrowing the arteries that supply the heart. That's gene, protein, cells, body. The classic mistake is calling it nutritional because fatty food raises cholesterol. Diet can add to it, but the cause is the gene.

scenes.title: 12. decision rule and handoff
scenes.narration: So for any non-infectious disease, first ask: can a pathogen pass it from person to person? If not, ask what changed first: a gene, an exposure, the diet, or control of cell division. Then trace the chain to the body. Next: how environmental exposures cause disease.

scenes.title: 13. key notes (quiet, about 60 seconds)
scenes.narration: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.title: 1. hook (a ban in 2003, cases today)
scenes.narration: Australia banned asbestos at the end of 2003. Yet each year, hundreds of Australians are still diagnosed with mesothelioma, a cancer that asbestos can cause. So how can a harm show up decades after the exposure stopped? And why do some people who breathed the same dust never get sick? That's today's question: how does environmental exposure cause disease?

scenes.title: 2. one spine for every case
scenes.narration: Earlier, you sorted the causes of non-infectious disease, and environmental causes come from outside the body. Here's how they actually make people sick. Every case follows one spine. First, an exposure: real contact with a harmful agent, including how much and for how long. Next, a change in cells or tissue. Then, an effect on health. Let's run tobacco smoke through it, because one exposure can lead to three different diseases.

scenes.title: 3. pathway one: lung cancer
scenes.narration: Pathway one is lung cancer. Smoke carries carcinogens, chemicals that raise the risk of cancer. They reach the cells lining the airways and attach to their DNA. You've seen what happens next: if that damage is copied before it's repaired, it becomes a mutation. When mutations build up in genes that control cell division, a cell can start dividing when it shouldn't. That can be the start of a tumour.

scenes.title: 4. pathway two: COPD
scenes.narration: Pathway two doesn't need a mutation at all. Smoke irritates the airways, so they stay inflamed for years. White blood cells gather and release enzymes that digest the thin walls between the tiny air sacs. Many small sacs merge into fewer, bigger ones, so there's much less surface for gas exchange. Mucus builds up too, because the hair-like cilia that sweep it out are damaged. Together this is COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and the lost walls don't grow back.

scenes.title: 5. pathway three: heart and blood vessels
scenes.narration: Pathway three is in the blood vessels. Chemicals in smoke damage the smooth lining of the arteries. Fatty deposits and white blood cells build up at those damaged spots, forming a plaque that narrows the artery. Meanwhile, carbon monoxide from the smoke takes oxygen's place on haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen, and nicotine makes the heart beat faster. A narrowed artery and a harder-working heart raise the risk of a heart attack or stroke.

scenes.title: 6. dose
scenes.narration: So what decides how much risk? First, dose: how much of the agent gets in, over how long. For smoking, it's counted in pack-years, packs per day multiplied by years smoked. One pack a day for twenty years is twenty pack-years. Think of each exposure as a ticket in a lottery you don't want to win. Most tickets lose, because the damage is repaired. But more tickets mean more chances that one cell collects several unlucky changes.

scenes.title: 7. latency, and the asbestos answer
scenes.narration: Second, time. Those changes take years to build up, so there's usually a long gap between exposure and diagnosis, called latency. Asbestos shows it clearly. Its fibres are long and thin, and once breathed in, they can lodge in the lining around the lungs. Immune cells called macrophages try to swallow them, can't, and keep releasing reactive chemicals that damage nearby cells and their DNA. That slow damage can take twenty to fifty years to become mesothelioma, which is why the 2003 ban hasn't stopped new cases yet.

scenes.title: 8. risk, not certainty
scenes.narration: So why do many heavy smokers never get lung cancer, while some people who've never smoked do? Because exposure raises the probability, not the certainty. DNA repair works better in some people than others. The immune system destroys some damaged cells. And which cell collects which mutation is partly chance. Never-smokers can be exposed in other ways too, through second-hand smoke, radon gas or polluted air. And exposures can add up: asbestos and smoking together raise lung cancer risk far more than either alone.

scenes.title: 9. a risk, not a verdict
scenes.narration: That's also why a risk isn't a verdict on one person. Many exposures aren't chosen: a worker cutting asbestos sheeting, or a child breathing a parent's smoke. What reliably lowers disease is lowering exposure across a whole population. Australia's daily smoking rate has fallen to around one adult in ten, and lung cancer rates in men have fallen too, decades behind. For UV, SunSmart's advice works the same way: slip, slop, slap, seek and slide.

scenes.title: 10a. attempt one (two trends, decades apart)
scenes.narration: Two exam questions. First. The graph shows the percentage of Australian men who smoked, and the rate of new lung cancer cases in men, from 1945 to 2020. Describe how the timing of the two trends differs. Then explain the difference. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 10b. feedback, item one
scenes.narration: Smoking fell steadily from 1945, but lung cancer kept rising until the early 1980s, then fell, decades behind. The explanation is latency. Mutations from earlier smoking were already building up, so cancers kept appearing long after people quit or never started. The classic mistake is saying smoking can't cause lung cancer because the two peaks don't line up.

scenes.title: 10c. attempt two (a named UV case)
scenes.narration: Second. A gardener has worked outdoors in Queensland for thirty years without sun protection. Explain how this repeated UV exposure can increase the risk of melanoma. Then explain why a co-worker with similar exposure may never develop it. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 10d. feedback, item two
scenes.narration: UV is absorbed by DNA in skin cells and joins neighbouring bases, so the DNA kinks. If that's copied before it's repaired, it becomes a mutation, and thirty years of exposure let mutations build up in genes that control division. But exposure raises the probability. Repair, immune clearance and chance differ between people. The classic mistake is writing that UV always causes cancer.

scenes.title: 11. decision rule and handoff
scenes.narration: So for any environmental disease question, name the exposure and its dose, describe the change in cells or tissue, link it to the effect, then explain why it's a risk, not a certainty. Next, an exposure nobody can avoid: what we eat, and how nutrition changes disease risk.

scenes.title: 12. key notes (quiet, about 60 seconds)
scenes.narration: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.title: 1. hook (two eras of nutritional disease)
scenes.narration: A century ago, Australian doctors still treated children for rickets, where growing bones soften and bend, and scurvy, where gums bleed and wounds won't heal. Today, the nutrition-linked diseases that fill our hospitals are mostly type 2 diabetes and heart disease. One set comes from too little, the other mostly from too much. So how does what we eat change disease risk?

scenes.title: 2. one chain for every nutrient
scenes.narration: Earlier, you saw that nutrition is one acquired cause of disease. Here's the chain that explains any case. Start with the nutrient and its normal job in the body. Then ask what changes when there's too little for long enough, a deficiency, or too much over many years, an excess. Then link that change to the effect. A deficiency takes away a job. An excess overloads a system that normally works.

scenes.title: 3. iron: the worked chain
scenes.narration: Take iron. Iron sits at the centre of haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. If you take in or absorb too little iron for long enough, your body makes less haemoglobin, and new red cells come out smaller and paler. Each litre of blood now carries less oxygen. During exercise, your muscles need more oxygen than the blood can deliver, so you tire quickly and get breathless. That's iron-deficiency anaemia.

scenes.title: 4. vitamin C and vitamin D
scenes.narration: The same chain works for vitamins. Vitamin C is needed by the enzymes that build strong collagen, the rope-like protein that holds together gums, skin and blood vessel walls. Without it, new collagen is weak, so small vessels leak, gums bleed and wounds heal slowly. That's scurvy. Vitamin D lets your gut absorb calcium. Without it, growing bones don't harden properly, so they can bend under the body's weight. That's rickets. Scurvy has a C in it, for vitamin C. Rickets needs daylight, because your skin makes vitamin D in sunlight.

scenes.title: 5. iodine: a loop that can't fix a missing ingredient
scenes.narration: Iodine adds a twist you'll recognise from homeostasis. Your thyroid gland uses iodine to build its hormones, which set how fast your cells use energy. With too little iodine, those hormone levels fall. Negative feedback responds: the pituitary releases more TSH, thyroid-stimulating hormone, telling the thyroid to work harder, and the gland grows. But the missing ingredient is still missing, so it keeps enlarging into a goitre. That's one reason Australian bread has been made with iodised salt since 2009.

scenes.title: 6. excess: insulin resistance
scenes.narration: Now excess, and type 2 diabetes. Remember what insulin does: it binds to muscle and fat cells, and that signal moves glucose transporters into the membrane, so glucose gets in. Years of taking in more energy than you use, with little activity, build up body fat, especially around the liver and other organs. Muscle, liver and fat cells then respond less to insulin. Insulin still binds, but fewer transporters move, so glucose stays in the blood. That's insulin resistance.

scenes.title: 7. beta cells cover, then fall behind
scenes.narration: At first, the beta cells in the pancreas cover for it by releasing more insulin, so blood glucose can stay close to normal for years. That's why many people don't know anything's wrong. Over time, the beta cells may not keep up, and blood glucose stays high. That's type 2 diabetes. Years of high glucose damage blood vessels, from tiny ones in the eyes, kidneys and nerves to the arteries feeding the heart. When the Australian AusDiab study tested adults, about half of those with diabetes hadn't been diagnosed.

scenes.title: 8. a risk factor, not a certain outcome
scenes.narration: So does eating too much cause type 2 diabetes? Not on its own. Compare scurvy: one missing nutrient, and the disease follows reliably until vitamin C is restored. Type 2 diabetes is different. Excess intake is a risk factor, something that raises the chance of disease without guaranteeing it. Family history, age, activity, sleep and some medicines change the risk too, and so does what food people can afford and reach. Heart disease is similar: saturated fat can raise LDL cholesterol, which helps build the plaque you saw with smoking, but it's one risk factor among several.

scenes.title: 9a. attempt one (a teenager indoors)
scenes.narration: Two exam questions. First. A fourteen-year-old spends almost all daylight hours indoors. Blood tests show low vitamin D, and their gut is absorbing little calcium. Using nutrient, change and effect, explain how this deficiency could affect their bones. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 9b. feedback, item one
scenes.narration: The nutrient is vitamin D, and its job is helping the gut absorb calcium. With little sunlight, the skin makes little vitamin D, so less calcium is absorbed. Growing bone doesn't harden properly and stays soft, so it can bend under the body's weight, which is rickets. The classic mistake is answering "drink more milk". Without vitamin D, extra calcium isn't absorbed well.

scenes.title: 9c. attempt two (reading the rates)
scenes.narration: Second. The chart shows new cases of type 2 diabetes per thousand adults each year, in four groups sorted by body weight and family history. Identify two risk factors the data show. Then explain why the claim "eating too much causes type 2 diabetes" overstates the evidence. Pause here to answer.

scenes.title: 9d. feedback, item two
scenes.narration: Obesity and a family history both raise the rate, and together they raise it most. But even in the highest group, about thirty in a thousand developed diabetes each year, so most didn't, and some healthy-weight adults did. Excess intake raises the chance, alongside other factors, so it's a risk factor, not a certain cause. The classic mistake is treating a higher rate as a guarantee.

scenes.title: 10. decision rule and handoff
scenes.narration: So for any nutrition question, name the nutrient and its normal job, say what changes with too little or too much, link it to the effect, then ask: is this one missing nutrient, or one risk factor among many? Next, what happens when cell division escapes control: how cancer begins and spreads.

scenes.title: 11. key notes (quiet, about 60 seconds)
scenes.narration: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.
